client:
I bombed my final project presentation last week, and I can't stop thinking about it. I felt so unprepared and flustered up there, and now I'm questioning if I'm even cut out for this major. Everyone else seemed so much more confident and polished than me. 

I guess I'm just not sure how talking about this will help - the grade is already in, so what's the point? I feel like I've proven I don't belong here.
therapist: It sounds like this experience has really shaken your confidence and left you feeling discouraged. Many people find it helpful to explore these kinds of situations because our thoughts about events often impact us more than the events themselves. What do you think might be the most painful part of this experience for you right now?

client: The most painful part is feeling like I'm not good enough compared to everyone else. I keep replaying the moment when I stumbled over my words and saw some classmates exchange looks - it's like they were thinking "why is she even here?" I know I'm probably overthinking it, but I can't shake the feeling that I don't belong in this program.
therapist: That moment of stumbling and seeing those looks clearly stuck with you deeply, and I can hear how much it's feeding that feeling of not belonging. Our brains often fixate on these perceived moments of judgment while overlooking all the times we've felt competent. What might be another way to interpret those exchanged looks you noticed?

client: I guess they could have been looking at each other for any reason - maybe one of them was passing a note or something. But it's hard not to take it personally when I was already feeling so exposed and vulnerable up there. Part of me knows I'm probably imagining the worst, but another part is convinced they were judging me.
therapist: It's completely understandable to feel that way when you're in such a vulnerable position - our minds often jump to the worst-case scenario in those moments. It's worth noting that you're already recognizing there might be other explanations, which shows some balanced thinking. How might your perspective shift if you imagined seeing another classmate stumble during their presentation?

client: If I saw someone else stumble, I probably wouldn't think much of it - I'd just feel bad for them and hope they weren't too embarrassed. But it's different when it's me - I feel like everyone will remember my mistake forever. I know logically that's probably not true, but it's hard to shake that feeling of being judged.
therapist: It's really insightful how you recognize you'd show compassion to others in that situation, yet struggle to extend that same kindness to yourself. That double standard we sometimes hold ourselves to can feel particularly painful. What might it feel like to try applying that same gentle understanding to yourself in this situation?

client: Honestly, the idea of being kind to myself about this feels uncomfortable - almost like I'd be making excuses for my failure. But I see what you mean about the double standard. It's just hard because my inner voice keeps saying "you should have prepared better, this is all your fault."
therapist: That inner critic can feel so convincing, especially when it's reinforcing beliefs we've held for a long time. It might help to notice how that voice of "you should have" actually makes it harder to learn from the experience. What do you think might happen if you tried responding to that critical voice with the same understanding you'd offer a friend?

client: I'd probably feel like I was being too easy on myself if I talked that way. But I guess telling myself "you're such a failure" hasn't exactly helped me improve either. It's just hard to find a middle ground between beating myself up and making excuses.
therapist: You're touching on something really important - finding that balance between accountability and self-compassion can indeed feel tricky. It's worth noting that being kind to ourselves doesn't mean ignoring areas for improvement, but rather creating a safer mental space to learn and grow. What would it look like for you to acknowledge what didn't go well while also recognizing the courage it took to get up there and present?

client: I guess I could acknowledge that I could have prepared better, but also recognize that everyone makes mistakes and it doesn't define my entire worth. It's just hard to believe that when I'm still feeling so embarrassed. I keep thinking about how much better everyone else did compared to me, and it makes me feel like I'll never measure up.
therapist: It's clear you're working hard to find that balanced perspective, even amidst the lingering feelings of embarrassment. Comparing ourselves to others can be particularly painful, especially when we're focusing on their highlights while seeing our own low points. What might shift if you considered that others might have their own hidden struggles and insecurities, even if they appeared confident?

client: I guess I never really thought about it that way - maybe some of those "confident" people were just better at hiding their nerves. I still feel like I stood out as the worst one though. It's hard to believe anyone else struggled as much as I did when I felt so obviously unprepared and flustered.
therapist: That feeling of standing out as "the worst" must be really painful to carry around. It's interesting how our minds can zoom in on our own struggles while assuming others' performances were flawless. What might change if you considered that your awareness of your own nervousness might actually mean you're more in touch with your emotions than others?

client: I never thought about my nervousness that way - I've always seen it as a weakness. But I guess being aware of my emotions could be a strength in some situations. It's just hard to see it that way when I'm so focused on how much I struggled compared to everyone else. I still feel like I need to "fix" this part of myself to be successful.
therapist: You're beginning to recognize there might be value in your emotional awareness, even though it's still challenging to see it as strength right now. It's understandable to want to "fix" perceived weaknesses, but sometimes what needs shifting is our perspective rather than ourselves. How might your approach to presentations change if you worked with your nervousness rather than against it?

client: I guess I could try to see my nervousness as a sign that I care about doing well, rather than just a weakness to overcome. But it's hard to imagine actually using it to my advantage - I've always thought I needed to completely eliminate it to be successful. The idea of working with it instead of against it feels unfamiliar and kind of uncomfortable.
therapist: What a meaningful insight - recognizing that your nervousness might actually be tied to how much you care. That discomfort you're feeling with this new approach makes complete sense when it challenges beliefs you've held for a long time. What small step could you imagine taking to start exploring this different relationship with your nervousness?
